abstract: This paper investigates a two-patch metapopulation model with asymmetric dispersal, motivated by the directional transport of organisms between populations by aquatic currents. We consider a system of ordinary differential equations in which dispersal is population-conserving but directionally asymmetric, and each patch is subject to a strong Allee effect: Populations below a critical threshold decline toward extinction, whereas those above the threshold persist and approach their carrying capacities. We analytically prove the convergence of solutions to equilibria, and identify parameter regimes in which positive equilibria necessarily exist. We then numerically explore the one- and two-parameter steady-state bifurcation structures with respect to combinations of asymmetric dispersal rates and the Allee threshold. In particular, for sufficiently high Allee thresholds, we identify broad parameter regions in which the extinction equilibrium is the unique equilibrium of the system. These extinction regions arise from the interplay between asymmetric dispersal and the Allee effect and, notably, are absent in the corresponding population-conserving dispersal model without an Allee effect. Our results demonstrate that, through 'rescue' effects and emergent extinction regimes, directional dispersal can fundamentally help or hinder population persistence in systems subject to the Allee effect, highlighting important implications for the conservation and restoration of endangered species experiencing asymmetric dispersal.
